estTime: 335 min syllabus teaching allocation + retrieval practice (not a measured completion estimate)
learningObjectives: FL-5.2.3 (K2): Risk analysis and test scope

topics.title: Official chapter 5 — Managing the Test Activities

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Chapter keywords: explain, distinguish and exemplify

elements.text: These are original plain-language explanations, not quotations from the official glossary. For each term, give a new example and explain its difference from a neighboring term. Use the official glossary with the CTFL syllabus context for authoritative wording.

rows: Record, analyze, classify, track and communicate anomalies and confirmed defects through their lifecycle.
Information enabling another person to understand, reproduce, assess and resolve an anomaly.
Preconditions that should hold before a specified activity begins.
Conditions used to judge completion of a specified activity, with unmet quality targets made visible.
A potential problem in the quality or behavior of the delivered product.
A potential threat to successful execution of the project, such as staffing or supplier delay.
An uncertain adverse event characterized by its likelihood and consequences.
Identify and assess risks so decisions can consider their nature and level.

Categorize already identified risks, estimate likelihood, impact and level, prioritize them and propose responses. Identification is the separate activity that produces the risk list; both belong to risk analysis.
Choose and carry out responses and monitor how risk changes.
Determine which adverse events or quality problems could matter in the context.
An assessed measure combining likelihood and impact under a defined model.
Coordinate identification, assessment, responses and monitoring of risks.
Actions intended to reduce the likelihood or consequences of an adverse event.
Track known risks, responses and new evidence or emerging risks over time.
Use product risk information to guide scope, depth, techniques, effort and priority.
The context-specific way testing will meet its objectives, including levels, types, techniques and resources.
A summary of completed testing, outcomes, deviations, residual risks and lessons.
Adjust the work in response to status and objectives; distinguish action from monitoring.
Observe and assess test status and progress to support control and reporting.
A communication artifact describing the test work's objectives, scope, approach, resources and schedule.
Develop and maintain the decisions and coordination needed to reach test objectives.
An ongoing status account of progress, impediments, deviations, risks and proposed actions.
A model favoring many fast narrow tests and fewer slow broad tests to balance feedback and coverage.
General guidance about how testing is carried out, informing context-specific plans and approaches.
A model classifying tests on business/technology focus and support-team/critique-product purpose.

elements.text: Official exam weighting: 9/40 questions (22.5%). Work in short topic blocks; retrieve before rereading. The chapter quiz contains 32 original questions across all objectives of this chapter. Revisit high-confidence errors with Smart Review and use the full official chapter and keywords to check completeness.
K3 application objectives here: FL-5.1.4, FL-5.1.5, FL-5.5.1. Practise them on paper with the Try first exercises until you can solve unseen examples without hints.

elements.description: A plan communicates objectives, scope, basis, approach, roles, assumptions, risks, resources, schedule and reporting. Update it as context changes; it does not remove uncertainty.

elements.text: Worked example: A shared plan records what an external payment outage means for testing and who decides on mitigation.
Close the notes: What should stakeholders learn from the test plan?

elements.description: Testers help refine testable stories and criteria, analyze risks, estimate effort and plan activities at release and iteration scales.

elements.text: Worked example: During refinement a tester identifies missing test data and estimates the testing tasks.
Close the notes: Recall how a tester contributes before implementation begins.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: FL-5.1.3 · Entry and exit criteria · K2

elements.description: Entry criteria express prerequisites to begin an activity; exit criteria express completion expectations. If time ends before quality targets are met, communicate residual risk and obtain stakeholder acceptance.

elements.text: Worked example: A ready environment is an entry condition; required coverage and acceptable open-defect risk are exit conditions.
Close the notes: Classify a criterion by the activity boundary it controls.

elements.description: Use relevant historical ratios, extrapolation from current observations, Wideband Delphi or three-point estimation. In Wideband Delphi experts estimate independently, discuss differences, then re-estimate until consensus; Planning Poker is a card-based Agile variant. For three-point use E=(a+4m+b)/6 and SD=(b-a)/6; effort and calendar duration differ.

elements.text: Worked example: With a=4, m=7 and b=16 person-days, E=8 and SD=2. Parallel staffing does not automatically divide calendar time exactly.

rows: Apply the historical test/development effort ratio to comparable work.
Use an explicitly stated model, such as recent comparable iteration means.
Collect isolated estimates; discuss when they fall outside the agreed range, re-estimate in isolation and repeat to consensus. Planning Poker is a card-based variant.
Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic expert estimates
Use the stated weighted mean and spread model; retain assumptions and effort units.

elements.text: Technique-selection check: experts first estimate in isolation, discuss estimates outside the agreed range and privately estimate again. This is Wideband Delphi; using numbered effort cards is its Planning Poker variant. Taking a numerical mean of recorded iteration effort is extrapolation, not expert consensus.

elements.title: Ratio and three-point estimates
elements.prompt: Historical development:test effort is 4:1, and comparable development work is 240 person-hours. A different task has three-point estimates a=3, m=6, b=15 person-days. Calculate the ratio estimate, then E = (a + 4m + b)/6 and SD = (b − a)/6. Keep the units.
elements.solution: Ratio estimate = 240 × 1/4 = 60 person-hours. E = (3 + 24 + 15)/6 = 7 person-days; SD = (15 − 3)/6 = 2 person-days, written as 7 ± 2 person-days (5 to 9). The spread alone is not a guaranteed completion interval. Neither result gives calendar duration without availability, dependencies and other scheduling assumptions.

elements.title: Extrapolation
elements.prompt: The last three iterations needed 18, 22 and 20 test hours for comparable scope. Using their mean as the model, estimate the next iteration and state one assumption.
elements.solution: (18 + 22 + 20)/3 = 20 test hours. Assumption: the next iteration has comparable scope, team and conditions. If that changes, the extrapolation model no longer applies without adjustment.

elements.text: Close the notes: Calculate an estimate, state its unit and identify its assumptions.

elements.description: Order tests by risk, coverage contribution or stakeholder priority as requested. Respect dependencies and resources. Additional coverage prioritization recalculates new coverage after every selection.

elements.text: Worked example: T1 covers A,B; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D. After T1, both T2 and T3 add one new item, so an explicit tie-breaker is needed.

elements.title: Additional coverage with a dependency
elements.prompt: A test is eligible only after its prerequisite has run. Order the tests in the table above by additional coverage among eligible tests. Break equal contributions by the lower test number.
elements.solution: T1 first (3 new items). T3 becomes eligible and adds 2. T4 adds 1. T2 adds 0. Order: T1, T3, T4, T2. Ordering by total coverage would put T2 ahead of T4; additional coverage must be recalculated after every selection.

elements.title: Risk-based order with a dependency
elements.prompt: T1 is Low risk. T2 is High risk but needs T3 to run first. T3 is Medium risk. T4 is High risk. At each step, run the highest-risk test whose prerequisite has already run; break equal risk by the lower test number. Derive the order.
elements.solution: T4 first (High and eligible). T2 is High but not yet eligible, so its prerequisite T3 runs next (Medium beats Low). Then T2, then T1. Order: T4, T3, T2, T1. A high-risk test cannot run before a mandatory prerequisite.

elements.text: Close the notes: Derive an order from the stated strategy and document ties rather than guessing.

elements.description: The pyramid typically has many fast, small, isolated tests and fewer slow, broad end-to-end tests. Layer labels vary; use the model to balance feedback speed and breadth.

elements.text: Worked example: A team moves repeated business-rule checks from slow UI flows into fast component tests while preserving essential user journeys.
Close the notes: Recall what changes from the bottom to the top of the pyramid.

elements.description: The quadrants combine business/technology focus with support-team/critique-product purpose. Q1 technology supports the team; Q2 business supports the team; Q3 business critiques the product; Q4 technology critiques the product. They are not lifecycle stages.

elements.text: Worked example: Business acceptance examples support implementation in Q2; a load test critiques technical behavior in Q4.
Close the notes: Classify a test on both axes and avoid treating quadrants as execution order.

elements.description: Risk combines likelihood and impact. Numeric risk levels may use likelihood multiplied by impact when scales permit; qualitative labels need a defined comparison model.

elements.text: Worked example: A likelihood of 0.2 and a EUR 50,000 loss imply EUR 10,000 expected exposure under that model.
Close the notes: Recall the two attributes and distinguish a scoring model from a probability guarantee.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: FL-5.2.2 · Product and project risks · K2

elements.description: Product risks concern quality of the delivered product. Project risks concern execution of the project, such as staffing, supplier delays or environment availability; one can influence the other.

elements.text: Worked example: An incorrect interest calculation is a product risk; losing the test specialist before release is a project risk.
Close the notes: Classify risks by what is at risk, not who reports them.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: FL-5.2.3 · Risk analysis and test scope · K2

elements.description: Risk analysis combines identification and assessment. Identification produces a list using workshops, interviews, brainstorming or cause-effect diagrams. Assessment categorizes already identified risks, estimates likelihood, impact and level, prioritizes them and proposes responses. Use the results to choose scope, priority, techniques, coverage and effort; revise the analysis as evidence changes.

elements.text: Worked example: A high-impact refund risk receives deeper negative and boundary testing than a low-impact cosmetic preference.
Close the notes: Explain how a risk assessment changes test depth rather than merely test order.

elements.description: Risk control combines risk mitigation and risk monitoring. Respond through mitigation, acceptance, transfer or contingency planning as appropriate. Testing reduces uncertainty and can support mitigation; it does not itself fix defects or eliminate all risk.

elements.text: Worked example: A critical defect triggers a fix and targeted regression while stakeholders assess residual release risk.
Close the notes: Separate a test action, a corrective action and a risk acceptance decision.

elements.description: Metrics can describe progress, execution outcomes, coverage, defects, risk and effort. State denominators and context; a pass rate is not a direct measure of overall product quality.

elements.text: Worked example: 80 passed of 100 executed gives an 80% execution pass rate, even when 200 tests were planned.
Close the notes: Recall useful metrics and state the denominator of each percentage.

elements.description: Progress reports support ongoing control with current status, impediments and next actions. Completion reports summarize outcomes, deviations, residual risk and lessons for the completed activity; tailor detail to the audience.

elements.text: Worked example: A daily report explains blocked tests; a completion report summarizes remaining risk at the end of the release test cycle.
Close the notes: Choose report content for its timing, purpose and decision maker.

elements.description: Use audience-appropriate reports, dashboards, meetings or informal discussion. Communicate urgent blockers and risk changes promptly, with evidence and proposed actions.

elements.text: Worked example: An executive needs business impact and a decision request; a developer needs reproduction data and environment details.
Close the notes: Translate the same issue for a business sponsor and a technical colleague.

elements.description: Identify and version test objects and testware, control changes and preserve baselines and traceability. Reproducing a result needs the matching build, configuration, data and tests.

elements.text: Worked example: A failure on build 12 cannot be reproduced confidently using an unknown build and newer test data.
Close the notes: List the configuration items needed to reproduce a test run.

elements.description: Write a concise title, reproducible steps, build and environment, data, expected and actual results, supporting evidence, severity, priority and references. Severity describes impact; priority expresses urgency to fix.

elements.text: Worked example: A payment defect report specifies currency, amount, build, steps and observed discrepancy rather than saying payments are broken.

elements.title: Report a stock defect
elements.prompt: Acceptance criterion AC-3: cancelling a Pending order sets it to Cancelled and restores its reserved stock once. Build 4.2, Chrome 130. You are signed in as the owner of Pending order O17 (2 reserved units; available stock 8). You cancel once. The status becomes Cancelled, but available stock becomes 12. Draft a defect report that another tester can reproduce without asking you questions.
elements.solution: Title: “Cancellation restores reserved stock twice”. Environment: build 4.2, Chrome 130. Preconditions: signed in as owner; O17 Pending, reserved 2, available 8. Steps: open O17 and cancel once. Expected: Cancelled and available stock 10 (AC-3). Actual: Cancelled and available stock 12. Attach timestamped before/after evidence and reference AC-3 and the test identifier. Assess severity from the inventory impact; agree priority with the responsible stakeholders. The tracking tool normally records the ID, reporter, date and initial status: check they are present. The observation does not prove which component caused it.

elements.text: Close the notes: Select or prepare a report that lets a different person reproduce and assess the anomaly.
Attempt these after studying the chapter, without looking at the keyword table. Explain each answer in your own words, then open the solution.

elements.title: Product risk versus project risk
elements.prompt: Classify: (1) a key tester is unavailable for two weeks; (2) search may respond too slowly under peak load; (3) a supplier delivers a component late; (4) a payment calculation may be wrong.
elements.solution: Project risks: (1) and (3). They affect the management and control of the project. Product risks: (2) and (4). They concern product quality characteristics.

elements.title: Parts of risk management
elements.prompt: Place each activity in risk analysis (identification or assessment) or risk control (mitigation or monitoring): identifying risks in a workshop; rating each risk by likelihood and impact; adding tests for a high risk; checking whether a mitigation is working.
elements.solution: Identifying risks in a workshop: risk identification. Rating likelihood and impact: risk assessment, which determines the risk level. Both are part of risk analysis. Adding tests: risk mitigation. Checking that the mitigation works: risk monitoring. Mitigation and monitoring are part of risk control.

elements.title: Entry versus exit criteria
elements.prompt: “The test environment is available and the story is ready for testing” and “All high-risk tests have passed and the defined coverage is achieved”. Which is an entry criterion and which an exit criterion?
elements.solution: The first is an entry criterion: a precondition for starting an activity. The second is an exit criterion: what must be achieved to declare the activity complete. In Agile, entry criteria are often called the Definition of Ready and exit criteria the Definition of Done.

elements.title: Monitoring, control and reports
elements.prompt: A test manager (1) collects pass/fail and coverage data daily; (2) reassigns testers to a blocked area; (3) sends a weekly status summary; (4) summarizes the results when testing ends. Classify each.
elements.solution: (1) Test monitoring. (2) Test control: guiding actions based on monitoring information. (3) Test progress report. (4) Test completion report.

elements.title: Test pyramid versus testing quadrants
elements.prompt: Classify these tests into testing quadrants: a component test, tests derived from user-story examples, a usability test and a performance test. Then state what the test pyramid says about the number of tests at its lower layers.
elements.solution: Component test: Q1 (technology-facing, supports the team). Tests from user-story examples: Q2 (business-facing, supports the team). Usability test: Q3 (business-facing, critiques the product). Performance test: Q4 (technology-facing, critiques the product). In the test pyramid, lower layers have many small, fast, isolated tests, and higher layers have fewer, more complex tests.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.1 · Test plans
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A test plan is immutable and removes uncertainty about resources, scope and schedules.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: A plan communicates objectives, scope, basis, approach, roles, assumptions, risks, resources, schedule and reporting. Update it as context changes; it does not remove uncertainty. Self-check: What should stakeholders learn from the test plan?

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.2 · Planning contributions
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A tester contributes to planning only after the story has been implemented.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Testers help refine testable stories and criteria, analyze risks, estimate effort and plan activities at release and iteration scales. Self-check: Recall how a tester contributes before implementation begins.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.3 · Entry and exit criteria
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Reaching a deadline proves the quality-related exit criteria are met.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Entry criteria express prerequisites to begin an activity; exit criteria express completion expectations. If time ends before quality targets are met, communicate residual risk and obtain stakeholder acceptance. Self-check: Classify a criterion by the activity boundary it controls.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.4 · Effort estimation
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The simple mean is the weighted three-point estimate, or person-days directly equal calendar duration.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use relevant historical ratios, extrapolation from current observations, Wideband Delphi or three-point estimation. In Wideband Delphi experts estimate independently, discuss differences, then re-estimate until consensus; Planning Poker is a card-based Agile variant. For three-point use E=(a+4m+b)/6 and SD=(b-a)/6; effort and calendar duration differ. Self-check: Calculate an estimate, state its unit and identify its assumptions.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.5 · Test prioritization
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A test's original total coverage remains its additional coverage after other tests have run.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Order tests by risk, coverage contribution or stakeholder priority as requested. Respect dependencies and resources. Additional coverage prioritization recalculates new coverage after every selection. Self-check: Derive an order from the stated strategy and document ties rather than guessing.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.6 · Test pyramid
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The test pyramid requires a large UI-heavy suite or prohibits integrated tests entirely.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The pyramid typically has many fast, small, isolated tests and fewer slow, broad end-to-end tests. Layer labels vary; use the model to balance feedback speed and breadth. Self-check: Recall what changes from the bottom to the top of the pyramid.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.1.7 · Testing quadrants
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Testing quadrants are four chronological stages that must execute in numeric order.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The quadrants combine business/technology focus with support-team/critique-product purpose. Q1 technology supports the team; Q2 business supports the team; Q3 business critiques the product; Q4 technology critiques the product. They are not lifecycle stages. Self-check: Classify a test on both axes and avoid treating quadrants as execution order.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.2.1 · Risk attributes
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Impact and likelihood mean the same thing, or a risk score is automatically a probability.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Risk combines likelihood and impact. Numeric risk levels may use likelihood multiplied by impact when scales permit; qualitative labels need a defined comparison model. Self-check: Recall the two attributes and distinguish a scoring model from a probability guarantee.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.2.2 · Product and project risks
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Any risk reported by a tester must be a product risk rather than a project risk.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Product risks concern quality of the delivered product. Project risks concern execution of the project, such as staffing, supplier delays or environment availability; one can influence the other. Self-check: Classify risks by what is at risk, not who reports them.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.2.3 · Risk analysis and test scope
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Risk analysis affects only execution order and never depth, technique or scope.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Risk analysis combines identification and assessment. Identification produces a list using workshops, interviews, brainstorming or cause-effect diagrams. Assessment categorizes already identified risks, estimates likelihood, impact and level, prioritizes them and proposes responses. Use the results to choose scope, priority, techniques, coverage and effort; revise the analysis as evidence changes. Self-check: Explain how a risk assessment changes test depth rather than merely test order.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.2.4 · Product risk responses
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Recording a risk or finding a defect automatically fixes it and removes the risk.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Risk control combines risk mitigation and risk monitoring. Respond through mitigation, acceptance, transfer or contingency planning as appropriate. Testing reduces uncertainty and can support mitigation; it does not itself fix defects or eliminate all risk. Self-check: Separate a test action, a corrective action and a risk acceptance decision.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.3.1 · Test metrics
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A pass percentage is meaningful without its denominator and proves overall product quality.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Metrics can describe progress, execution outcomes, coverage, defects, risk and effort. State denominators and context; a pass rate is not a direct measure of overall product quality. Self-check: Recall useful metrics and state the denominator of each percentage.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.3.2 · Test reports
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Progress and completion reports serve identical decisions at identical times.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Progress reports support ongoing control with current status, impediments and next actions. Completion reports summarize outcomes, deviations, residual risk and lessons for the completed activity; tailor detail to the audience. Self-check: Choose report content for its timing, purpose and decision maker.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.3.3 · Communicating test status
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Every audience should receive the same unexplained raw logs, and urgent risk changes can wait.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use audience-appropriate reports, dashboards, meetings or informal discussion. Communicate urgent blockers and risk changes promptly, with evidence and proposed actions. Self-check: Translate the same issue for a business sponsor and a technical colleague.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.4.1 · Configuration management
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The latest build and data are always sufficient to reproduce a historical failure.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Identify and version test objects and testware, control changes and preserve baselines and traceability. Reproducing a result needs the matching build, configuration, data and tests. Self-check: List the configuration items needed to reproduce a test run.

examPitfalls.title: FL-5.5.1 · Defect reporting
examPitfalls.trapDescription: High priority makes a vague report reproducible, and severity always equals urgency to fix.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Write a concise title, reproducible steps, build and environment, data, expected and actual results, supporting evidence, severity, priority and references. Severity describes impact; priority expresses urgency to fix. Self-check: Select or prepare a report that lets a different person reproduce and assess the anomaly.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Stakeholders ask what is excluded, which risks matter and who reports progress. Which artifact should communicate this?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The plan coordinates scope, risks and responsibilities. Logs, counters and screenshots provide narrower evidence.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A major supplier dependency changes during testing. What should the team do with its plan?

options.text: Wait until completion to tell stakeholders
Keep every plan detail fixed regardless of impact
Replace all planned tests with supplier assurances
Reassess assumptions and update the approach and communication

practiceQuiz.rationale: A plan must remain useful as context changes. Fixed assumptions, unsupported substitution and delayed communication undermine it.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is a typical tester contribution during iteration planning?

options.text: Assess testability and estimate test tasks

practiceQuiz.rationale: Testers contribute test expertise to planning. Business authority, all fixes and legal approval are not implied by the role.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which contribution is useful during release planning?

options.text: Identify product risks and a test approach across iterations
Postpone all testing estimates until code is complete

practiceQuiz.rationale: Release planning benefits from risk and approach input. Deferred estimates, impossible guarantees and owning all design details do not describe the contribution.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A condition says the environment and test data must be ready before execution begins. What is it?
practiceQuiz.rationale: This prerequisite controls starting execution. Exit criteria control ending an activity; severity concerns defect impact.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Time expires while critical risks remain. What is the appropriate basis for ending testing?

options.text: Communicated residual risk and stakeholder acceptance
A claim that the clock proves quality
Reclassification of all unexecuted cases as passed

practiceQuiz.rationale: A time limit can end work with informed risk acceptance. It does not prove quality or justify falsifying defects or outcomes.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Three-point estimates are a=3, m=6 and b=15 person-days. What is the expected effort?
practiceQuiz.rationale: E=(3+4×6+15)/6=42/6=7. The simple average is 8; the most likely value alone is 6.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Historical development:test effort is 3:2. A comparable project has 180 development person-days. What test effort is estimated?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Testing is 180×2/3=120. Reversing the ratio gives 270; subtracting or assuming equality does not apply the given model.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Risk scores are T1=9, T2=4 and T3=7 with no dependencies. What is descending risk priority?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Descending score is 9,7,4. The other orders either invert priority or place a lower score ahead of a higher one.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E. After selecting T1, which adds more new coverage?
practiceQuiz.rationale: After T1, T2 adds nothing while T3 adds D and E. Additional coverage is recalculated against already covered items.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is typical near the base of the test pyramid?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The base emphasizes fast, small checks; slower broad tests sit higher. Release decisions are not a test layer.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why avoid placing every business-rule check in the UI end-to-end layer?

options.text: Component tests prove business acceptance alone
UI tests cannot detect any defects
Broad tests usually provide slower, more costly feedback

practiceQuiz.rationale: Broad tests have a role but should be balanced with faster checks. The model neither forbids them nor equates component testing with acceptance.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Business-facing acceptance examples guide implementation. Which quadrant fits?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Q2 is business-facing and supports the team. Q1 is technology/support, Q3 business/critique and Q4 technology/critique.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A technical load test critiques the product. Which quadrant fits?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Q4 combines technology focus and product critique. The other quadrants differ on one or both axes.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which two attributes determine risk level in a common risk model?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Likelihood and impact characterize risk. Administrative counts, report size and version/date identifiers are not substitutes.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A quantitative model uses probability 0.1 and impact EUR 80,000. What expected exposure follows?
practiceQuiz.rationale: 0.1×80,000=8,000. Impact alone ignores probability; division and an extra factor of ten produce the other errors.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which is a project risk?

options.text: The test environment may arrive two weeks late
The product may lose saved orders
The login may expose personal data
The product may calculate interest incorrectly

practiceQuiz.rationale: Environment delivery threatens project execution. The other risks concern delivered product quality.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which is a product risk?

options.text: The supplier may deliver a tool late
The test budget may be reduced
The senior tester may leave the project
A refund may be applied twice

practiceQuiz.rationale: Duplicate refunds concern product behavior. Staffing, supplier schedule and budget are project risks, although they can affect product risk indirectly.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A payment error has high likelihood and severe impact. How should this influence testing?

options.text: Run the shortest test first regardless of coverage
Use deeper relevant coverage and suitable techniques
Assume a large test count alone mitigates the risk

practiceQuiz.rationale: Risk analysis should shape depth and scope, not just speed or counts. Cosmetic focus does not target the payment risk.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: New evidence lowers one risk and raises another. What should happen?

options.text: Reassess priorities and the test approach
Convert the raised risk into a passed result
Ignore evidence after the plan is approved
Freeze the original ranking until the next project

practiceQuiz.rationale: Risk analysis evolves with evidence. Approval is not a reason to ignore change, and a risk is not a test outcome.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A stakeholder knowingly accepts a documented residual risk. Which response is this?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Acceptance is an explicit decision to tolerate risk. Testing does not eliminate risk by itself; confirmation and identification are different activities.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Tests expose a severe defect. Which action most directly mitigates its product risk?

options.text: Record more passing tests in unrelated features
Correct the defect and verify the change and relevant regressions
Rename the failed test as informational

practiceQuiz.rationale: Correction addresses the cause and verification checks the result. Cosmetic reporting changes and unrelated counts do not remove the defect.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Of 100 planned tests, 60 ran and 45 passed. What is the pass rate among executed tests?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Executed-test pass rate is 45/60=75%. 45% uses planned tests as denominator; 60% is execution progress; 25% is the executed non-pass fraction.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which is a test coverage metric?

options.text: Number of team members at a meeting
Total lines in a status email

practiceQuiz.rationale: Requirement coverage measures exercised basis items. Attendance, company age and message length do not measure test coverage.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A release test cycle has ended. Which content belongs in its completion report?

options.text: Outcome summary, residual risks and lessons learned
A guarantee that production will have no defects
A list of all employee performance rankings

practiceQuiz.rationale: Completion reporting consolidates outcomes and remaining risk. Guarantees and employee ranking are inappropriate; future tasks alone do not summarize completion.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which content is especially useful in an ongoing progress report?

options.text: Only the final archived testware location
An unqualified statement that all work is done
A product advertisement unrelated to test evidence
Current deviations, blockers and corrective actions

practiceQuiz.rationale: Progress reports support control during work. Archiving belongs to completion context; unsupported closure and advertising do not inform status.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A critical environment outage blocks testing today. What communication is appropriate?

options.text: Wait for the final completion report
Promptly notify affected stakeholders with impact and needed action
Mark blocked cases as passed to keep the dashboard green
Send the same raw log to every audience without context

practiceQuiz.rationale: Timely audience-appropriate communication supports decisions. Delays, false results and unexplained logs impede them.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A sponsor asks whether remaining risks threaten launch. What should a tester emphasize?

options.text: The number of report pages produced
Business impact, evidence and the decision needed
Every stack frame before stating the impact

practiceQuiz.rationale: Sponsors need actionable risk information. Technical details may support it but do not replace impact; page counts and blame are not useful status evidence.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which record best supports reproducing a failed test?

options.text: Only the number of passing tests last month
Build, configuration, data and test version used

practiceQuiz.rationale: Reproducibility depends on matching configuration items. Personnel names, aggregate counts and dates alone do not reconstruct a run.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why establish a test baseline?

options.text: To prove that no defects remain
To identify an approved, reproducible set of related artifacts
To prevent every future controlled change

practiceQuiz.rationale: A baseline identifies a controlled configuration. Changes remain possible through control; correctness and traceability are separate concerns.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: On build 22, the requirement subtracts a 10% discount from USD 1.25 and rounds to cents using decimal round-half-up. The application displays USD 1.12. Which report best supports reproduction?

options.text: Build 22; apply a discount to an unspecified price; expected correct rounding, actual lower amount; attach a screenshot
Build 22; enter USD 1.25, add 10% tax; expected USD 1.13, actual USD 1.12; attach steps and evidence
Build 22; enter USD 1.25, apply 10% discount; expected USD 1.13 using round-half-up, actual USD 1.12; attach steps and evidence
Build 22; enter USD 1.25, apply 10% discount; expected USD 1.12 using round-half-up, actual USD 1.12; attach steps

practiceQuiz.rationale: The exact decimal result after discount is 1.125, which rounds half-up to 1.13. A useful report preserves the discount operation, data, rounding rule and discrepancy. Tax, a wrong oracle or unspecified inputs would misdescribe or obscure this anomaly.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Build 23 accepts decimal-comma amounts in locale fr-FR. In Firefox, entering 1,50 and saving should retain 1.50, but displays 150.00. Which defect report best enables another tester to reproduce this?

options.text: Build 23, Firefox, en-US; enter 1.50 and save; expected 1.50, actual 150.00; attach stored-value evidence
Build 23, Firefox; enter an unspecified amount and save; expected a decimal value, actual an inflated value; attach screenshot
Build 23, Firefox, fr-FR; enter 1,50 and save; expected 1.50, actual 150.00; attach stored-value evidence
Build 23, Firefox, fr-FR; enter 1,50 and save; expected 150.00, actual 150.00; attach stored-value evidence

practiceQuiz.rationale: The report with fr-FR and the comma input retains the failure trigger and correct expected/actual values. Changing locale or input tests a different scenario; expecting 150.00 removes the discrepancy; unspecified data makes reproduction less reliable.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

quickRecap.value: A plan communicates objectives, scope, basis, approach, roles, assumptions, risks, resources, schedule and reporting. Update it as context changes; it does not remove uncertainty.
Testers help refine testable stories and criteria, analyze risks, estimate effort and plan activities at release and iteration scales.

Entry criteria express prerequisites to begin an activity; exit criteria express completion expectations. If time ends before quality targets are met, communicate residual risk and obtain stakeholder acceptance.

Use relevant historical ratios, extrapolation from current observations, Wideband Delphi or three-point estimation. In Wideband Delphi experts estimate independently, discuss differences, then re-estimate until consensus; Planning Poker is a card-based Agile variant. For three-point use E=(a+4m+b)/6 and SD=(b-a)/6; effort and calendar duration differ.

Order tests by risk, coverage contribution or stakeholder priority as requested. Respect dependencies and resources. Additional coverage prioritization recalculates new coverage after every selection.
The pyramid typically has many fast, small, isolated tests and fewer slow, broad end-to-end tests. Layer labels vary; use the model to balance feedback speed and breadth.

The quadrants combine business/technology focus with support-team/critique-product purpose. Q1 technology supports the team; Q2 business supports the team; Q3 business critiques the product; Q4 technology critiques the product. They are not lifecycle stages.
Risk combines likelihood and impact. Numeric risk levels may use likelihood multiplied by impact when scales permit; qualitative labels need a defined comparison model.
Product risks concern quality of the delivered product. Project risks concern execution of the project, such as staffing, supplier delays or environment availability; one can influence the other.

quickRecap.key: FL-5.2.3 · Risk analysis and test scope
quickRecap.value: Risk analysis combines identification and assessment. Identification produces a list using workshops, interviews, brainstorming or cause-effect diagrams. Assessment categorizes already identified risks, estimates likelihood, impact and level, prioritizes them and proposes responses. Use the results to choose scope, priority, techniques, coverage and effort; revise the analysis as evidence changes.

Risk control combines risk mitigation and risk monitoring. Respond through mitigation, acceptance, transfer or contingency planning as appropriate. Testing reduces uncertainty and can support mitigation; it does not itself fix defects or eliminate all risk.
Metrics can describe progress, execution outcomes, coverage, defects, risk and effort. State denominators and context; a pass rate is not a direct measure of overall product quality.

Progress reports support ongoing control with current status, impediments and next actions. Completion reports summarize outcomes, deviations, residual risk and lessons for the completed activity; tailor detail to the audience.
Use audience-appropriate reports, dashboards, meetings or informal discussion. Communicate urgent blockers and risk changes promptly, with evidence and proposed actions.
Identify and version test objects and testware, control changes and preserve baselines and traceability. Reproducing a result needs the matching build, configuration, data and tests.

Write a concise title, reproducible steps, build and environment, data, expected and actual results, supporting evidence, severity, priority and references. Severity describes impact; priority expresses urgency to fix.
